summary:
Loreto is a department of Peru and stands under the national framework: Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

No trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement finding for Loreto appears in the sources. Every attached item is national in scope, and as national law the restrictions below apply in Loreto.

Facility access is restricted by statute. On 2 April 2025 the Congress plenary approved, exempt from a second vote, the dictamen of the law strengthening the right to sexual integrity of children and adolescents, whose article 5 bars from public sanitary facilities anyone whose biological sex does not match the facility's intended sex, with exceptions limited to accompanying or assisting minors, patients or people with specific needs. The February 2025 committee stage covered bills 6506 and 8457, which would bar entry to facilities destined to the sex opposite one's birth sex, with exceptions for custody, medical care or accompanying an adult, a child under 12 or a disabled person, and would require unambiguous signage. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

The restriction reaches private life as well as public facilities. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV told Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, to 'go use the men's room'. Trans-rights activist Gianna Camacho warns that security staff would judge people by personal criteria, such as requesting their DNI, so the practical effect is broader than the text of the rule.

Hate-crime protection is absent. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The TLGBI Rights Observatory recorded 54 killings of LGBTI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru between 2020 and 2023, with trans women most affected and hate crimes rising. In February 2023 trans woman Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, was kidnapped in central Lima and murdered in Carabayllo with approximately 30 gunshots at the hands of the 'Los Gallegos' gang; the body showed gunshots, stab wounds and throat-slitting indicating extreme hate. The observatory's co-author Gianna Camacho states that recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

One protective outcome is on record. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack; it was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history.
tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights, a standard the April 2025 facility provision does not meet.

IDEHPUCP, the human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, published an analysis of the facility ban by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte on 15 April 2025. They argue that the measure implicitly brands trans people as more prone to entering bathrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, conditions basic rights on verifiable 'biological sex', and violates equality, non-discrimination and gender self-determination. The institute also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

The same legislative package bans inclusive language, and Congress again rejected equal marriage. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.
localsOnly:
Residents of Loreto live under the national facility rule rather than any departmental ordinance, so the article 5 restriction, its narrow exceptions and the signage requirements bind Loreto's public authorities, malls, gyms and clinics on the same terms as the rest of the country.

Screening falls on staff and officials. Gianna Camacho's warning that security personnel would apply personal criteria, including demands to see a DNI, describes the everyday mechanism by which a trans resident is identified and refused, and a consumer-protection body has already declined to act on a complaint brought by a trans woman turned away from a gym.

Local health services in Loreto operate under guidance revised in June 2024, which removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity and is described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings.

The inclusive signage ban affects Loreto businesses, schools and municipal offices directly, since wording such as 'women in their diversity' is now prohibited, and the raised obscenity minimum of four years applies to local prosecutions.

Reporting of incidents remains thin. The 54 killings and 170 rights-violation cases recorded between 2020 and 2023 are national totals, and the observatory's co-author Gianna Camacho states that these figures are only a sub-registry.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records a Loreto-specific trans ordinance, departmental enforcement action or court challenge, so the absence of a regional finding reflects what was supplied rather than a verified finding that none exists.

Whether the article 5 facility restriction has been enforced in Loreto, and by which authorities, is not sourced. The gym complaint and the television harassment cited here occurred outside the department and are used as evidence of how the national policy operates.

The 54 killings and 170 rights-violation cases are national aggregates; a departmental breakdown for Loreto is not sourced, so the local level of violence remains unresolved.

Implementation of the unambiguous-signage requirement and of the inclusive-signage ban in Loreto is not documented in the inventory, and no source confirms whether the April 2025 provisions have been litigated in Loreto's courts.
